newsitem.title: USA: Major U.S. bankers group still wants legal reforms.
newsitem.headline: Major U.S. bankers group still wants legal reforms.

text.p: A leading bank trade group reiterated on Tuesday its support for overhauling U.S. financial regulations after a Washington newspaper said the industry's support for reform was waning.

American Bankers Association has been a leading supporter of updating the laws, but the group's top lobbyist was quoted in Tuesday's Washington Post as saying banks "don't think they necessarily need a financial modernization bill right now."
In a letter dated June 3, the lobbyist, Ed Yingling, said the article may have left a "misleading impression."

"As you prepare to mark up financial modernization legislation, I want to reiterate ABA's willingness to work with you," Yingling said in the letter addressed to House Banking Committee chairman Jim Leach, Republican of Iowa.

The bankers would oppose some versions of bank reform, however, Yingling said. A proposal that left in place separate federal charters for banks and savings and loans institutions would be unacceptable to banks, he said in the letter.
Leach said at a hearing Tuesday his committee would produce a new bank reform bill by Friday incorporating pieces of earlier proposals for a markup starting next week.

For more than a decade, Congress has debated eliminating the legal separation between banks and other financial services contained in the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act and other laws. The efforts have never succeeded, in part because the banking, securities and insurance industries could not reach a consensus about how the laws should be changed.

Legislators began the 105th Congress with renewed optimism, but hopes have dimmed somewhat in the past two months as the old controversies have arisen again. Tuesday's Washington Post article was seen as yet another sign that support for reform was fading.
Some saw controversy ignited by the Clinton administration's bank reform proposal, announced last month.

"I thought we were making progress," New Jersey Republican Marge Roukema said at the opening of Tuesday's bank committee hearing. "But I am deeply disturbed by the evident reports that this proposal has opened new divisions -- chasms between interest groups which I had thought were being brought together."
